Prose for the `Reading the numbers` section of evals.html. It sat as five hand-authored paragraphs in the page, OUTSIDE every `content:evals-*` region — the one part of that page nothing regenerated — and it drifted from the table directly above it. Every figure it quotes is now a `{{evals:…}}` placeholder.

WHY THE PLACEHOLDERS ARE NOT SUBSTITUTED HERE: scripts/check-boundaries.mjs forbids scripts/ from referencing evals/, so build-content.mjs cannot read evals/results.json and must not learn how. The prose therefore ships as a TEMPLATE in content/dist/content.json, and evals/run.mjs — which already has both content (through lib/knowledge/index.js) and the numbers it just produced — substitutes and writes the region. Direction stays content → lib/knowledge → evals.

WHY IT IS NOT A CHUNK: it is prose about the evaluation, not prose about Yordan. It is emitted as a top-level `evalsPage` field, is derived into no chunk, and is absent from `manifest` — so neither the build-vectors corpus hash nor `corpus.manifestChars` in results.json moves when it changes.

reading._placement: evals.html section 04, inside `<div class="ev-prose">`. The region markers do not exist yet — adding them and consuming this field is evals/run.mjs's change, not the content build's.
paragraphs: **Plain lexical search won on ranking, and the structured arm lost.** BM25 reaches {{evals:bm25.hit3}} hit@3 and {{evals:bm25.mrr}} MRR; navigating by name reaches {{evals:tools-only.hit3}} and {{evals:tools-only.mrr}}. The design being evaluated here expected the opposite, and the number is reported the way it came out. The reason is visible in the failures: a name match fires on whichever entity happens to share a word with the question, and on questions phrased the way people actually phrase them — *“what user research methods does he use?”* — no entity is named at all. The corpus is small, single-author and lexically consistent, which is precisely the condition under which BM25 is strong.

**Knowing when to say nothing is where they separate, and it is not close.** BM25 abstains on {{evals:bm25.abstained}} of {{evals:abstention.total}} unanswerable questions. It returns a confident ranked list for *“did he ever work at Google?”* — the word appears eight times in the corpus, in Google Analytics, Google Play and Google AI Studio, none of them an employer — and for *“what are his salary expectations?”*, and for *“does he speak Japanese?”*. The tools arm abstains on {{evals:tools-only.abstained}} of {{evals:abstention.total}}, because no entity was named. That is not a tuning artefact; it is the difference between matching words and resolving identifiers.

**Fusing the two rankings made both worse.** Tools-first with BM25 appended scores {{evals:hybrid.hit3}} hit@3 — below BM25 alone — and abstains on nothing, because the fallback always fires. It inherits the weaker ranking *and* the weaker judgement. That result killed the originally proposed shape, which is the most useful thing this table did.

**What the failure suggested instead.** Stop fusing rankings and split responsibilities: let the name match decide *whether* the corpus covers the question, and let BM25 decide *what* comes back once it does. That arm — `tools-gated` — holds {{evals:tools-gated.hit3}} hit@3 and {{evals:tools-gated.separability}} separability, tied for best in the table, while raising the abstention rate to {{evals:tools-gated.abstain}}. Roughly seven points of ranking traded for the entire ability to say “not on file”. It is labelled post-hoc everywhere it appears, because it was written after seeing the first three arms on this same question set; it is a hypothesis this run suggests, not a result this run establishes, and it needs questions written after it to become one.

**Two holes in the corpus, found by the eval rather than by a reviewer.** Location, availability and contact details live in `content.json` as structured fields and appear in no chunk, so *“where is he based?”* cannot be answered by any search over prose — the only chunk containing the word “Sofia” is the education line, about Sofia University, and BM25 duly returns something else entirely. Separately, the 2007–2009 quality assurance role has no bullet points, so the content build produced no chunk for it at all: the role is in the index and invisible to search, and every arm scores zero on it. Both are why the tool layer reads structured fields directly instead of searching for them.

**One question no arm could answer, and it is the case for embeddings.** *“How far has he run?”* shares no term with *“42 km. Marathon finisher.”* — lexical search returns nothing at all. That is the exact shape of question a semantic retriever exists for. The embeddings arm has since been run: it answers this question and wins every retrieval class, at {{evals:embeddings.hit3}} hit@3 against BM25's {{evals:bm25.hit3}}. The argument became a measurement.

**The point the corpus statistics make on their own.** The complete table of contents — every project id, title, client, tag and one-line summary, every role and span — is a few thousand characters. It fits in the system prompt. A retriever exists to solve “I cannot enumerate what is in here”; when the whole index fits in the prompt, that problem does not exist, and provisioning a stateful, billed service to solve it anyway is a decision about a résumé rather than about a corpus. That argument survives this table. The claim that structured lookup also *ranks* better did not.
reading._placeholderNote: `format` names the formatter already in evals/run.mjs: `pct` is `(x*100).toFixed(1)+'%'`, `num` is `x.toFixed(3)`. `abstained` is a COUNT, not a rate — `Math.round(arm.abstain * questions.abstention)` — because the sentence says "abstains on N of 11". `total` is `questions.abstention`. A substituter that finds a `{{evals:…}}` token with no entry here, or an entry whose token never appears, should fail the build: an unfilled placeholder rendering literally on the page is exactly the class of defect this move exists to end.
reading._reviewNote: Claims in the paragraphs above that NO placeholder can carry, because they are judgements about a table rather than cells of it. They were reproduced verbatim, unaltered, and listed here so the OWNER decided the wording; each now carries a `resolution` recording the decision he returned and the wording that replaced it. The entries are kept rather than deleted, so a phrase that changed has a reason on file and not only a diff. The rule is unchanged: an agent must not invent a replacement sentence — every replacement below is the owner's own.

review.was: true of 0.869 separability when three arms were measured
review.now: tools-gated separability is 0.920 and gated-embeddings ties it exactly — it is joint best, not best
review.cannotInterpolate: a superlative is a comparison across rows; substituting a number does not fix the word
review.resolution: RESOLVED — owner's wording, applied. The phrase now reads "tied for best in the table". The separability figure stays a placeholder; only the qualitative claim moved.

review.was: "the full 72.7%" — the tools arm's own rate, carried over intact
review.now: tools-gated abstains at 90.9%, which is HIGHER than the tools arm's 72.7%, so "the full" no longer describes what happened
review.cannotInterpolate: the figure interpolates; the word "full" is the claim and it is now wrong in the reader's favour
review.resolution: RESOLVED — owner's wording, applied. The clause now reads "while raising the abstention rate to {{evals:tools-gated.abstain}}". The number is still interpolated; only the words around it changed.

review.phrase: The embeddings arm is built and gated behind an API key rather than run, so this remains an argument rather than a measurement, and the table says so instead of guessing.
review.was: true when the arm was skipped
review.now: the embeddings arm ran: six published metrics, 93.0% hit@3, and it is the page's hero stat
review.cannotInterpolate: the sentence asserts the absence of a measurement that now exists — replacing it is authoring, not interpolation
review.resolution: RESOLVED — owner's wording, applied. The sentence now reads "The embeddings arm has since been run: it answers this question and wins every retrieval class, at {{evals:embeddings.hit3}} hit@3 against BM25's {{evals:bm25.hit3}}. The argument became a measurement." Both figures are placeholders rather than typed digits, so this sentence cannot drift from the table the next time the eval is re-run — which is the failure it is replacing. `{{evals:embeddings.hit3}}` is the twelfth placeholder and is new with this change.

review.phrase: tied for best in the table
review.was: the owner's replacement for "the best in the table", correct when tools-gated and gated-embeddings both measured 0.920 separability
review.now: OPEN. This is the third time this one clause has been falsified, and it is now wrong for a second, independent reason: evals/CLAUDE.md excludes separability from the columns an arm is allowed to lead, because awarding it a win counts the abstention rate twice. So there is no longer a defensible reading of "best" on this metric at all.
review.cannotInterpolate: a superlative is a comparison across rows; substituting a number does not fix the word, which is why correcting the value three times has not stopped it breaking
review.resolution: OPEN — needs the owner. Tracked as item 30, whose instruction is to remove the claim SHAPE rather than correct the value again. An agent must not author the replacement (see _reviewNote), so the clause is left standing and reported. The minimal change consistent with item 30 is deletion of the four words, which asserts nothing new.

review.phrase: Roughly seven points of ranking traded for the entire ability to say “not on file”.
review.was: true when tools-gated held 30.6% hit@3 against BM25's 37.4% and BM25 abstained on nothing
review.now: OPEN, and wrong twice over. BM25 gained a stopword list, so it now holds 83.7% hit@3 against tools-gated's 34.7% — the trade is 49 points, not seven. And BM25 now abstains on 43.8% of the unanswerable questions by itself, because a query made only of function words yields no scoring term, so tools-gated no longer confers "the entire ability" to abstain.
review.cannotInterpolate: "seven points" is a difference between two cells and "the entire ability" is a claim about one arm having none of a capability; neither is a metric this file can carry as a placeholder without a new formatter
review.resolution: OPEN — needs the owner. Both figures exist as placeholders already ({{evals:tools-gated.hit3}} and {{evals:bm25.hit3}}), so a wording that states the two numbers instead of their difference would be re-run-proof — but choosing that wording is authoring, not interpolation.

review.phrase: and for “what are his salary expectations?”, and for “does he speak Japanese?”
review.was: true when BM25 had no stopword list and scored on any query term at all
review.now: OPEN. Both questions now tokenise to content words only — [salary, expectations] and [speak, japanese] — none of which appears in the corpus, so BM25 returns NOTHING for both. They are now examples of the opposite of what the sentence uses them for. The third example survives: “did he ever work at Google?” still returns eight results, because `google` is genuinely in the corpus nine times.
review.cannotInterpolate: the sentence names specific questions and asserts a behaviour for them; no placeholder can carry a worked example
review.resolution: OPEN — needs the owner. Caused by the stopword list, which is a retrieval improvement (+16pp hit@3) that made two of this paragraph's three illustrations obsolete. Reported rather than rewritten. Whichever examples replace them should be chosen from the seven questions BM25 still answers confidently, which evals/results.json lists.

review.phrase: the word appears eight times in the corpus, in Google Analytics, Google Play and Google AI Studio, none of them an employer
review.now: OPEN, and independent of the stopword change: `google` occurs 10 times across 9 chunks (df=9). The reasoning is untouched — none of the occurrences is an employer — only the count is stale.
review.cannotInterpolate: a corpus term frequency is interpolatable in principle, but there is no placeholder source for one today; adding a `term` source would make this class of claim safe permanently
review.resolution: OPEN — needs the owner for the wording, though this one is a plain figure correction rather than a judgement. Worth noting as the argument for a `{{evals:term.google.count}}`-style placeholder source: this is the only figure in the prose that no gate can currently reach.
